title: The monk at Bosra
hook: the sirah tells of a Christian monk, Bahira, who saw signs in the boy on a caravan to Syria

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shepherd, and a flock in the hills. Your line was: every prophet was a shepherd.

A stone cell by the trade road near Bosra, on the edge of Syria. Caravans from Mecca have passed it often, and the monk inside has never spoken to them, the sirah says. This time he does. He sends word to the travelers: I've prepared food, and I want every one of you to come, young and old, slave and free. The merchants of Quraysh look at each other. What's changed? Today: Bahira.
screen: `A MONK'S CELL BY THE ROAD.` → `HE NEVER SPOKE TO THEM BEFORE.` → `"EVERY ONE OF YOU, COME."`

segments.voice: The caravan belongs to Abu Talib, and he has brought his nephew, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, still a boy. Ibn Ishaq tells the story. The monk is named Bahira, a Christian who, the sirah says, had learned from a book kept in that cell. From his window he has seen something: a cloud shading one traveler as the caravan came in, and a tree bending its branches over him where he sat. At the meal, the boy isn't there. He's been left with the baggage, the youngest. Bahira insists: bring him. Then he watches him closely, and asks him questions. When Bahira asks in the name of al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the idols of Mecca, the boy refuses to be asked by them. Bahira asks in God's name instead, and the boy answers. Finally the monk looks at his back and sees a mark between his shoulders. Bahira turns to Abu Talib with a warning: take your brother's son home, and guard him carefully. And Abu Talib does. How should this be heard? Carefully. Al-Tirmidhi records a version of the journey too, and some hadith scholars have questioned parts of it, so it's honest to hold the details lightly. What stays is the shape. On a dusty road, a stranger from another faith looked closely at an orphan boy left with the bags and saw something worth protecting. The sirah keeps this Christian monk in the story with respect, as a neighbor who recognized goodness when it walked in.
screen: `A CLOUD, A BENDING TREE.` · `"BRING THE BOY."` · `HE WON'T SWEAR BY THE IDOLS.` · `"TAKE HIM HOME AND GUARD HIM."` · then, large: `SOMEONE SAW IT EARLY.`

segments.voice: Think back to someone who saw something good in you before you saw it yourself, a teacher, a coach, an older cousin, a stranger even, and let their face and their words come back. Then turn it around: is there someone near you, left with the bags, so to speak, whose goodness no one has named yet? If you pray, you can ask Allah to open your eyes to it; if not, just hold that person in mind.
Bahira. A Christian monk on the road to Syria, who, the sirah says, saw signs in the boy and told Abu Talib to guard him. Today's word.
Your line: someone saw it early. Tomorrow, the league of the virtuous. Until then.

screen: `DAY 713 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LEAGUE OF THE VIRTUOUS.`

chat.says: What did the monk Bahira tell Abu Talib about his nephew?
options: To take the boy home and guard him carefully; the sirah says he saw signs in him.
To bring the boy back every year, so the monk could watch him grow.
To settle in Syria, far from the idols and the people of Mecca.
chat.meaning: In Ibn Ishaq's telling, Bahira saw signs, then warned Abu Talib: take your brother's son home, and guard him carefully.

Bahira.meaning: a Christian monk near Bosra, in the sirah

Bosra.meaning: a town on the trade road, on the edge of Syria

al-Lat.meaning: one of the idols of Mecca

al-'Uzza.meaning: another of the idols of Mecca

Abu Talib.meaning: the Prophet's uncle, who led the caravan

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Abu Talib's caravan to Syria; Bahira at Bosra)
Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3620 (the journey with Abu Talib and the monk)

notes: The boy's age (sirah: about nine or twelve) is left out under the claims rule.
Details (the cloud, the tree, the questions by al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the mark between the shoulders, 'never came out before') follow Ibn Ishaq; confirm.

Tirmidhi 3620 number and grading cited from memory; the script says only that 'some hadith scholars have questioned parts of it' (e.g., the mention of Abu Bakr and Bilal in that version). Confirm framing.
Bahira is described respectfully as a Christian monk and 'neighbor'; no comparison of traditions is made. A Keeper may wish to check that this sits well for Christian listeners too.
'The mark between his shoulders' is the seal of prophethood in the sources; the script doesn't name it as such. Confirm.

Editor: 'passed it for years... never once come out' became 'passed it often... never spoken to them', closer to Ibn Ishaq; 'books' became 'a book'; cut 'before anyone in Mecca saw anything special', which contradicted days 707 and 710 and was not in the source. Ibn Ishaq's warning also names a group to guard him from; the script keeps only 'guard him', deliberately.
